clue.text: Admit to city where old vicarage was

blocks.note: to grant a point is to admit it
Chester is a cathedral city in north-west England

explanation.surface: Someone owning up to the city where an old vicarage once stood.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Brooke's poem 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester' names the village near Cambridge, so the definition points at the poem's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Grantchester, a village outside Cambridge, is the setting of Rupert Brooke's famous poem about its old vicarage.

clue.text: Mean to assert how old one is

blocks.note: to aver is to state firmly
your age is how old you are

explanation.surface: Someone intending to state their age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean to' reads as 'intend to', but Mean is a noun or adjective standing alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics the mean is the ordinary arithmetic average of a set of numbers.

clue.text: Witnessed important game if that is 22's finale

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the final letter of that entry is wanted

blocks.note: a Test match is a major international cricket game
taken as written
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is
22 is 22-down, SYNOD

explanation.surface: Someone saw an important game, whatever 22's ending turns out to be.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match between national sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To have testified is to have given evidence as a witness, in court or elsewhere.

clue.text: Sound of activity round fair - theatrical nonsense

indicators.note: round means placed around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: a busy place hums
fair, in the sense of all right or acceptable

explanation.surface: The noise of a busy fairground, dismissed as showbiz claptrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fair' suggests a fairground, but here it means passable.
explanation.definitionFit: Hokum is stage business or sentimental claptrap used to win an audience, hence any nonsense.

clue.text: Quiet girl on Irish river

blocks.note: the sound used to ask for quiet
a girl's name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shy girl sitting beside a river in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shannon is the longest river in Ireland, flowing south-west to Limerick.

clue.text: Letter reveals record fibre production

blocks.note: an EP is an extended-play record
istle is a fibre produced from agave leaves

explanation.surface: A letter that discloses figures on fibre output.
explanation.walkthrough: Istle, a coarse fibre from Mexican agave plants, is a rare word that crosswords lean on.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal letter, as in the New Testament letters of the apostles.

clue.text: Fair sample of a kiss by some of the platoon

blocks.note: a kiss is written as a cross, X
a section is a subdivision of a platoon

explanation.surface: Soldiers in a platoon handing out kisses as a fair test.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-section is a representative sample taken across a whole population or group.

clue.text: Stranger's glasses

definitions.note: read as 'stranger is', a comparative adjective with a verb

blocks.note: first meaning: more odd is, using rum for odd
second meaning: large drinking goblets

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe looks possessive, the glasses of a stranger, but it is 'is'. Rum is old British slang for odd, so rummer means odder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rummers are large stemmed drinking goblets, and rummer is also the comparative of rum, odd.

clue.text: Can Queen frustrate such tricks?

blocks.note: surface reading: a question about thwarting some underhand schemes
setter's reading: in a card game, a queen can beat a jack in a trick, and tricky dealing is dishonest

explanation.walkthrough: The jack in a pack of cards is also called the knave, and a queen outranks it when tricks are won.
explanation.definitionFit: Knavish means dishonest or roguish, the behaviour of a rascal, and recalls the knave card.

clue.text: Robber destroying castle in England?

definitions.note: a phrase describing the job, where the answer is the noun for the worker

blocks.note: first meaning: a burglar who breaks into homes
second meaning: a demolition worker, since an Englishman's home is his castle

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'an Englishman's home is his castle' turns a demolition worker who knocks down houses into a castle-destroyer.
explanation.definitionFit: A housebreaker is both a burglar entering homes and a contractor who demolishes old buildings.

clue.text: One ruddy school head reversed lists of lessons

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is used
reversed means turned back to front, so the assembled string is read backwards

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
both are mild British euphemisms for bloody
the first letter of school

explanation.surface: A red-faced headteacher has turned around the timetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruddy and bally are old-fashioned British substitutes for the swear word bloody.
explanation.definitionFit: Syllabi, the plural of syllabus, are outlines of the topics a course of study covers.

clue.text: Spirit of brave fellow I outmanoeuvred

indicators.note: letters that are manoeuvred are moved about into new positions

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
taken as written
the word splits into out and manoeuvred: those three letters moved about

explanation.surface: A courageous man was beaten by a cleverer opponent.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word is read in two halves: out supplies the letters and manoeuvred tells you to move them. A brave is a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: Manitou is the supernatural power or spirit in Algonquian belief, so it belongs to a Native American brave.

clue.text: Do this with writ to initiate court proceedings

definitions.text: Do this with writ to initiate court proceedings

blocks.clueFragment: Do this with writ to initiate court proceedings
blocks.note: surface reading: delivering a writ to start a lawsuit
setter's reading: the tennis stroke that starts each point on the court

explanation.walkthrough: Both a legal document and a tennis rally get going with the same verb, and court fits the law and the game.
explanation.definitionFit: You formally deliver legal papers to a defendant, and in tennis this stroke opens every point.

clue.text: Hypocritical in the matter, because involved

indicators.note: something involved is wrapped up inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: in re is Latin legal shorthand for in the matter of
since can mean because

explanation.surface: Someone accused of two-facedness over some affair, for reasons that are tangled.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypocritical person does not mean what they say, so they are not sincere.

clue.text: Composer involved in theatricals? Not he!

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so the letters are mixed up
not means without, so those two letters are left out

blocks.note: taken as written
letters to remove

explanation.surface: A composer who refuses to take part in amateur dramatics.
explanation.definitionFit: Domenico Scarlatti and his father Alessandro were Italian Baroque composers of sonatas and operas.

clue.text: Tragic end as female forecaster of doom

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of tragic
taken as written
a woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman who predicted disaster comes to a tragic end herself.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a summary of the Trojan prophetess's fate, which makes the definition doubly apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassandra, the Trojan prophetess cursed never to be believed, gives her name to anyone predicting disaster.

clue.text: Skilful technique of one sort of fiction

blocks.note: first meaning: expertise or skill
second meaning: the word that goes before fiction for stories of the future

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition works by completing a phrase: the answer plus fiction names a genre.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean a craft mastered by skill, and science fiction is a familiar literary genre.

clue.text: Piece of music - Elgar left nothing out

indicators.note: out suggests being put out of order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
zero, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Elgar wrote a piece and omitted nothing from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left nothing out' reads as 'omitted nothing', but left and nothing are letters and out is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegro is a fast, lively movement or composition, named from its Italian tempo marking.

clue.text: Sort of 1 do who cuts things fine?

blocks.note: first meaning: 1 is 1-down, GAMBLER, and one kind plays at dice
second meaning: one who chops food into small cubes

explanation.walkthrough: 'do' is the old abbreviation for ditto, so it repeats 'sort of' before the second definition. The question mark marks the cook's sense as playful.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who plays dice is a kind of gambler, and a cook or gadget dicing vegetables cuts them small.

clue.text: Led astray like Marvell's mistress, caught in the act

indicators.note: something caught in another thing is trapped inside it

blocks.note: a deed is an act
Andrew Marvell's poem is 'To His Coy Mistress'

explanation.surface: A seducer misleads a reluctant mistress and is caught red-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: To be decoyed is to be lured into a trap by a bait or false signal.

clue.text: Restrict succinct approval of swindle?

blocks.note: a con is a swindle
a one-word OK

explanation.surface: Curbing a crook by briefly signing off on his scam.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, 'Con? Fine!', a terse go-ahead for a scam.
explanation.definitionFit: To confine is to keep within limits, as you restrict a prisoner or a discussion.

clue.text: These wall-hangings add a seasonal touch

definitions.text: These wall-hangings add a seasonal touch

blocks.clueFragment: These wall-hangings add a seasonal touch
blocks.note: surface reading: festive decorations or tapestries hung indoors
setter's reading: frozen drips hanging from walls and eaves in winter

explanation.walkthrough: Wall-hangings suggests tapestries, but these hang on the outside of a house in cold weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Icicles are tapering spikes of ice that form as dripping water freezes, a sign of winter.

clue.text: Council pronouncing offence extraordinary

indicators.note: pronouncing means saying out, so the words are judged by how they are spoken

blocks.note: an offence is a sin, and extraordinary is odd

explanation.surface: A council declaring some misdeed outrageous.
explanation.definitionFit: A synod is an assembly of clergy and church members that governs church affairs.

clue.text: A trap's set back in capital of this old region

definitions.text: A trap's set back in capital of this old region

blocks.clueFragment: A trap's set back in capital of this old region
blocks.note: surface reading: an ancient snare relocated to a regional capital
setter's reading: a mouth, slang trap, held in check, as in Sparta whose people were famously terse

explanation.walkthrough: Trap is British slang for mouth. Sparta was the capital of this Greek region, whose people gave us laconic, sparing of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconia was the ancient Greek region around Sparta, and its people were proverbial for brief speech.

clue.text: Figure it's a poor horse - no two ways about it

indicators.note: two ways means read forwards and then backwards as well
about means surrounding, so the outer letters go around the inner piece

blocks.note: taken as written
the same word used again, this time to be turned round

explanation.surface: A figure who insists, beyond argument, that a horse is useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No two ways about it' looks like a stock phrase meaning certainly, but no is used both forwards and backwards, wrapped around the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonagon is a plane geometric figure with nine straight sides and nine angles.

clue.text: Not the first offence for a subordinate

blocks.note: the one after the first
a fiddle is a fraud or swindle

explanation.surface: A court treating a minor's offence as no longer a first one.
explanation.walkthrough: A fiddle is British slang for a petty fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: To play second fiddle is to take a lesser role, so the phrase names someone in a subordinate position.
